extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students (U.S. patent litigation/practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts rules governing competency of witnesses, burden of proof, venue, federal equity and appellate jurisdiction, and procedures for interfering patents and repeal/annulment of patents under 19th-century U.S. statutes and case law. Focused on litigation posture and who may challenge or enforce patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency of licensee as witness
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee is a competent witness for the patent, in an action for an infringement, for he has no direct pecuniary interest in supporting the patent, but it may be for his advantage that it should not be supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees may testify for the patentee; their testimony is admissible though the court should consider possible motives or advantages that might bias them. Weight of such testimony may be limited by circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility of third-party declarations about prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where evidence of prior user by some third party is attempted to be shown, the declaration of such party as to his motives for such user are inadmissible as mere hearsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant cannot prove prior use through an unavailable third party's statements of motive; instead admissible evidence (documents, live testimony, other non-hearsay proof) must be used to establish prior user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff competence depends on state law on party examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, under the laws of any State, parties may be examined in their own behalf, the plaintiff, in an action for infringement brought in a district embracing such a State, is a competent witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a patentee (plaintiff) may testify in his own case turns on the local/state rule allowing party examination; federal courts in such districts will deem the plaintiff competent if state law permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on defendant for alien-patentee sale requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defence is set up that the patentee being an alien has not complied with §13 of the act of 1836, which requires that such patentee must put and continue on sale to the public, on reasonable terms, the invention for which the patent was granted, the burden of proof rests on the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant alleging noncompliance with statutory sale/offer conditions (for alien patentees) must prove that the patentee failed to put the invention on sale as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent procurement of extension: must be tried directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud in obtaining an extension of a patent can only be tried in a direct proceeding to impeach the patent, and not in a collateral proceeding, as in a suit in equity to recover for infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges alleging fraud in procurement/extension require a direct action to impeach the patent (e.g., suit to annul)—such issues are not to be litigated collaterally in ordinary infringement suits seeking damages or injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to grant patents including special/retrospective grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may pass general or special laws in favor of inventors; they may leave a particular inventor to the protection afforded by a general law, or they may pass a special law in his behalf, or they may exempt his case from the operation of a general law by extending his exclusive right beyond the term fixed by such general law. They may even grant to an inventor the exclusive right to his invention after the same has gone into public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special statutory grants are constitutionally permissible, but such enactments will not be construed to operate retrospectively (making prior lawful uses unlawful) without unmistakable statutory language; courts favor non-retroactive interpretations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts' original (and generally exclusive) jurisdiction over patent validity/force
rubrics_metrics.description: All actions, suits, controversies, and cases arising under any law of the United States, granting or confirming to inventors the exclusive right to their inventions or discoveries, shall be originally cognizable ... by the circuit courts of the United States ... which courts shall have power, upon bill in equity ... to grant injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the controversy turns on the validity or force of letters-patent, jurisdiction belongs to federal circuit/district courts (first instance) and on appeal to the Supreme Court; state courts generally have no cognizance where patent validity is in issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-court jurisdiction for contract disputes under patents
rubrics_metrics.description: But where the controversy at issue does not turn upon the letters-patent themselves, but rather upon the force of some contract under them, e.g. an assignment or license, which acknowledges their validity, in such cases the jurisdiction appertains ... to the State courts, and can only be brought into the United States courts on some other ground, e.g. that of citizenship or residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes that are essentially contract claims (specific performance, breach of license) that implicitly accept patent validity belong in state courts unless another federal ground (diversity, federal question separate from validity) exists; litigants should frame or plead issues accordingly to obtain or avoid federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee default can convert license into infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee, whose right is conditioned upon the weekly payment of a certain sum, and who neglects to pay the same, but who continues to use the invention, is virtually guilty of an infringement of the patent, and may, like any other infringer, be enjoined by a United States court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a license explicitly conditions continued use on payments, failure to comply may forfeit the licensee's defense and expose them to injunctions and other remedies for infringement; courts will consider contract terms and equitable adequacy of legal remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper venue: actions must be brought where defendant resides or is served; attachment insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Such action can only be brought in the district in which the defendant resides or in which he is personally served with the summons, and that the commencement of an action by attaching the property of a non-resident defendant was not sufficient to confer jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal service within the district or defendant residence is required for jurisdiction; foreign attachments and local State attachment practices do not automatically provide federal jurisdiction. Corporations are inhabitants of their charter state; presence of an agency/store and attaching goods in another district generally will not confer jurisdiction there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation venue: corporate existence tied to charter state
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation chartered under the laws of New Jersey, but having an agency and store in New York ... neither the levying of the writ of attachment upon the goods of the defendants in this district, nor the service of the summons upon their president within it ... have the effect to give jurisdiction to the court ... a corporation having no corporate existence out of the State under whose laws it is created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs should sue corporate patentees in the district of incorporation (or where service properly establishes jurisdiction), not rely on attachments or local agencies to confer federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court with personal jurisdiction may enjoin activity in other districts; actions against physical machines require local proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the court has jurisdiction of the person of the defendant, it may restrain him from violating the patent in a district other than the one in which the suit is brought. Still, where it may be necessary to proceed directly against the machine itself, as in cases of extreme contumacy or of fraudulent contrivance to evade an injunction, semble, proceedings must be instituted in the district in which the machine is located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal-jurisdiction-based injunctions can enjoin conduct nationwide (or in other districts), but direct remedies against specific physical property (seizure, sale) generally must be pursued where the property is located. Choose remedies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal equity jurisdiction includes post-expiration discovery and account
rubrics_metrics.description: The equity jurisdiction conferred upon the circuit courts by the act of 1836, § 17, is irrespective of the right of the plaintiff to an injunction or his demand for one. Consequently the patentee is entitled to a discovery and account after the expiration of the term for which the patent is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after patent term expiration, patentees may seek equitable discovery and accounting remedies for past infringements under federal equity jurisdiction; relief is not strictly limited to injunctions during the patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court appellate limits: amount-in-controversy for cost-only matters
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be stated that [Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction] does not extend by virtue of the act of 1836, § 17, to cases where the matter in controversy is, not the settlement of the claims and rights of a patentee, but the mere amount of costs. Such a question is left for decision under the provisions of the Judiciary Act of 1789, and consequently the amount in issue must exceed $2,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to the Supreme Court in patent cases may be limited when the only dispute is costs; plaintiffs/defendants should be mindful of statutory thresholds (subject to later modification by acts such as 1861) when considering appeal strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole case goes up when lower court sends matter under §17 discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: When a case is sent up to the Supreme Court, under the discretion conferred upon the court below, by the act of 1836, the whole case must go up; the word 'reasonable,' in the statute, applying rather to the cases themselves than to the points of the cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lower federal court certifies or sends a patent case under statutory discretion, expect the appellate review to encompass the entire case, not merely isolated issues; plan records and preserves of issues accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable relief for interfering patents (act of 1836): scope of relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of 1836 made provision for suits by bill in equity to declare void either of two interfering patents, or an existing patent where a subsequent applicant claimed the invention on the ground of priority ... The court was empowered, in the case of two interfering patents, to declare either of them void, in the whole or in part, or invalid or inoperative in any part or portion of the United States, according to the interest which the parties to the suit might possess in the inventions patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interference suits courts can adjudicate priority and may partially or wholly void patents or limit their operation geographically or by claim; relief is tailored to parties' interests and the scope of the interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference judgments affect non-parties only if direct and affirmative
rubrics_metrics.description: With regard to the effect of this proviso, it has been held that, in order to affect parties who were not parties to the suit for interference, the judgment must be direct and affirmative, declaring the interference and that one of the patents is void in the whole or in part, or inoperative, or invalid in some particular part of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To bind third parties, an interference judgment must clearly and affirmatively declare voidness or interference; advisory or incidental findings may not extinguish rights of non-parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1870 remedies: review by bill in equity for refused applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The case of an application for a patent finally refused, for any reason whatever, which, of course, includes a refusal on the ground of interference with an existing patent, is provided for under section fifty-two of the new act, by giving the applicant a remedy by bill in equity; which, in fact, operates as a review of the grounds on which the application was finally rejected, the adjudication under the bill being that the applicant is entitled to the patent, if it so appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants denied by the Patent Office (including for interference) may seek equitable review in federal court under the 1870 act; successful adjudication can operate to annul an existing patent insofar as the interference extends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sue to vacate/annul a patent: interference vs. fraud/mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the act of 1836 nor the act of 1870 has made provision for vacating or declaring void any existing patent excepting upon the ground of interference, and that too at the suit of some rival patentee, or applicant, or of some person claiming under them. Parties who are sued, or are liable to be sued as infringers ... are not embraced in these provisions. It has therefore been held by the Supreme Court ... that when it is sought to vacate or annul a patent, on the ground that it was obtained by a fraud on the government, a private individual cannot maintain a bill in equity in his own name. But ... the general chancery jurisdiction ... affords a remedy ... in the name of the attorney-general, on the relation of some one who is injured specially or as a part of the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct challenges to patents for fraud or mistake ordinarily must be brought by rival patentees/applicants (interference suits) or by the United States/attorney-general; private individuals lacking interference standing generally cannot maintain a chancery suit to annul on fraud grounds in their own name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy uncertainty for expired patents; attorney-general may seek annulment ab initio
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether this remedy can be resorted to in the case of a patent that has expired, is doubtful. ... it was held that the extended patent having expired before the bill was filed, there was no equity to support a suit to set it aside, because there was nothing for the bill to operate upon. But ... Mr. Justice Miller said that where the United States or the attorney-general shall institute a suit to have a patent declared null ab initio, which, though no longer in force as to present or future infringements, is used to sustain suits for infringements during its vitality, the question will be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing and remedy to attack expired patents are complex and fact-dependent; although an expired patent may limit equitable relief, the government (attorney-general/United States) may be able to seek annulment ab initio especially if the patent has been used to support suits for past infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference suit procedural limits as to effect and parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The court was empowered ... to adjudge the patent to the applicant, as the fact of priority of right or invention might appear; provided, that the adjudication should not affect the rights of any person except the parties to the action, and those claiming title from or under them subsequent to the rendition of the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference adjudications transfer rights between parties and their successors in interest as of the judgment date but generally do not operate to divest unrelated third parties; careful pleading and joinder are important to secure comprehensive relief.
